title: Comparative Analysis
text:
We wanted to know if there were higher barriers to healthcare access for certain demographics of people, specifically those who have a higher need for care or belong to disparaged communities. We chose the Research and Development Survey (RANDS 10) and the Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS 7) to look for this information. Both surveys are government data sets with substantial amounts of documentation which makes them both highly credible sources for looking for an answer to our research question.
In each data set, one row was one adult response to each respective survey. Both data sets also targeted the entire country, so there can be no comparisons between cities or states. The biggest ethical concern for both surveys are protecting participant’s privacy, making sure all responses remain anonymous, which both surveys seem to emphasize. The RANDS 10 documentation includes a codebook, README file, and technical documentation explaining an overview of the project, sampling methodology, and response rates. The HINTS 7 data source includes a Methodology Report, Public Codebook, Survey Overview and Data Analysis Recommendations, History Document, and Annotated Questionnaire. If we wanted to rely on the data source documentation to corroborate the data we were using in our research topic, the HINTS 7 source would likely have more of the concrete documentation we would want to lend credibility to our findings.
In terms of answering our originally posed research question, the HINTS 7 data set has a lot more of the kind of questions we wanted answered, such as people’s opinion on the quality of care they received, or the quality of communication of their healthcare providers. The RANDS 10 data set has a lot fewer of these kinds of questions and is mostly concerned with participant’s overall quality of health. However, both data sets have many questions related to various health conditions (such as cancer, asthma, arthritis) that could potentially be used as proxy variables for people having a higher need for care. What they both lack is nearly any questions related to whether or not participants faced any barriers to accessing healthcare reliably or within a reasonable amount of time.
Overall, if we had to choose only 1 data set, the HINTS 7 survey would probably stand a higher chance of holding up to scrutiny about the credibility of the data and actually providing the information required to answer our research question. Preferably, we could use both data sets with a series of well-considered proxy variables in an attempt to find either the answer to our question or some other interesting information that could potentially be used to answer a different research question.

Stated collection details


RANDS 10 was conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago in the spring of 2024. Data collection began on April 18, 2024, and ended on May 13, 2024. NORC invited 6,342 AmeriSpeak panel members to complete the questionnaire via web and phone administration. Of the panel members contacted, 5,017 completed the survey, resulting in a 79.1% completion rate (unweighted) and a weighted cumulative response rate of 15.8%.

title: Data Collection Facts Label
text:
Data Source Facts Label














Source Identity






Source name


Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) 7




Domain/topic


Health and healthcare experience




Source type


Federally funded public-use dataset











Collection Context






Collector/producer


The survey is administered by the National Cancer Institute, a public federal agency (part of NIH) and carried out by Westat, a private research corporation




Original purpose


To collect nationally representative data on the American public’s access to and use of health information, in order to improve health communication




Collection method


Mail survey; households got mailed a questionnaire and one adult filled it out themselves either on paper or online




Record-creation event


A sampled adult completes and returns the survey either by paper (mail) or online











Observation and Scope






Unit of observation


One adult’s survey response. Each row is one person’s answers about their health status, healthcare experiences, and background




Population or objects represented


Civilian, non-institutionalized adults (18+) living in the US




Time period covered


March 25 - Sept 16, 2024




Geographic area coverage


United States (national)











Variables and Data Structure






Main variables/fields


Chronic conditions/Health Status (MedConditions_Diabetes, MedConditions_HighBP, MedConditions_HeartCondition, MedConditions_LungDisease, EverHadCancer, GeneralHealth)




Provider communication (ChanceAskQuestions, ExplainedClearly, SpentEnoughTime, InvolvedDecisions)
Quality and trust (QualityCare, TrustHCSystem, DiscriminatedMedCare2)
Care coordination (ManageMultipleProviders, ProbCare_WaitLong2, ProbCare_RedoTest)
Access/Cost (HealthInsurance2, FreqGoProvider, DiffPayMedBills)
Demographics (Age, BirthSex, RaceEthn5, Education, IncomeRanges)




Data types included


Primarily categorical (yes/no), rating scales (never/sometimes/usually/always), a few numeric (age, height, weight), and IDs (anonymous household ID)




Direct measurements


Age, height, weight, education, household income range, whether they have health insurance (yes/no), number of provider visits in past year. All responses are self reported by respondent (not measured or verified)




Possible proxy variables


“Has a doctor ever told you that you had…” questions (MedConditions columns and EverHadCancer) may stand in for actually having the condition.
Self-rated health (GeneralHealth) may stand in for actual health status.
Care quality and provider communication ratings (QualityCare, SpentEnoughTime, ExplainedClearly, InvolvedDecisions) may stand in for the actual quality of care received.
Trust in healthcare system (TrustHCSystem) may stand in for past experiences with it.
Number of provider visits (FreqGoProvider), health insurance status (HealthInsurance2), and difficulty paying medical bills (DiffPayMedBills) may stand in for access to care











Documentation






Documentation found


Methodology Report, Public Codebook, Survey Overview and Data Analysis Recommendations, History Document, Annotated Questionnaire




Stated collection details


36k addresses were randomly selected from a national list of home addresses. Addresses were sorted into four groups (urban/rural and high/low minority population) and more were purposely picked from high minority and rural areas. One adult per household was chosen using the next birthday method. Households got up to 5 mailings, with $2 sent to everyone and larger payments offered to some. 7,585 surveys came back, and blank/incomplete/duplicates were dropped which left 7,278 (Response rate was ~27%). Returned paper surveys were scanned and web surveys were exported, then both were checked, cleaned, and combined into one dataset

title: Investigating a Dataset’s Ingredients
text: The topic we chose was on healthcare access. Specifically, we wanted to investigate whether certain demographics of people faced more barriers or an overall poorer experience when seeking or receiving healthcare. We chose it because we have a personal connection to this area, whether it’s ourselves or someone we know, when it comes to our less-than-ideal experiences in the healthcare system. For example (and a large reason we chose to look into this), we often noticed or experiemnced that having chronic illnesses on record has led to poorer experiences in healthcare, such as difficulty getting coverage for tests or being treated different by providers based on that information.
